summary.text: For \(p\ge7\), hockey-stick and binomial product formulas yield fifth-order \(p\)-adic expansions of the two factors about \(3\); reflection, stuffle, alternating-binomial, and Vandermonde identities for the resulting harmonic sums show that both corrections are divisible by \(p^3\) and that their weighted linear combination \(4c+3s\) is divisible by \(p^5\). Thus every nonlinear term in \((3+c)^4(3+s)^3\) is negligible modulo \(p^5\), while the cases \(p=3,5\) follow by direct finite evaluation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 S(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{n+k-1}{k}^{2}.
\]
By the hockey-stick identity,
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{n+k-1}{k}=\binom{3n}{n}
 \qquad(n\geq 1).
\]
Indeed, \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}=\binom{n+k-1}{n-1}\), and summing over \(k=0,\ldots,2n\) gives \(\binom{3n}{n}\). Thus, for positive \(n\),
\[
 a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{4}S(n)^{3}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 a(1)=3^4(1+1+1)^3=3^7=2187.
\]
We prove that \(a(p)-2187\) is divisible by \(p^5\) for every prime \(p\geq3\).

Throughout the main argument assume \(p\geq7\). We perform calculations in the localization of \(\mathbb Q\) at \(p\), or equivalently in \(\mathbb Q_p\). If \(x\) is such a rational number, write
\[
 x=O(p^r)
\]
to mean that its \(p\)-adic valuation is at least \(r\). The usual rules
\[
 O(p^r)+O(p^r)=O(p^r),\qquad O(p^r)O(p^s)=O(p^{r+s})
\]
will be used freely. Every denominator occurring below is a product of integers from \(1\) to \(p-1\), and is therefore a \(p\)-adic unit. At the end, an estimate \(a(p)-2187=O(p^5)\), applied to an integer, is precisely the assertion that \(p^5\mid a(p)-2187\).

For \(r\geq1\) and \(1\leq k\leq p\), put
\[
 H_r(k)=\sum_{1\leq i<k}\frac1{i^r},
 \qquad H_r=H_r(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\frac1{i^r}.
\]
We abbreviate
\[
 H=H_1,
 \qquad Q=H_2,
 \qquad C=H_3,
 \qquad R=H_4.
\]
We shall also need the nested sums
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 T&=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{H_1(k)}{k^2},
 &U&=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{H_2(k)}k,\\
 V&=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{H_2(k)}{k^2},
 &W&=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{H_1(k)}{k^3},\\
 X&=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{H_3(k)}k.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Let
\[
 e_2(k)=\sum_{1\leq i<j<k}\frac1{ij}
       =\frac{H_1(k)^2-H_2(k)}2,
\]
and define
\[
 E=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{e_2(k)}{k^2},
 \qquad A=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{H_1(k)^2}{k^2}.
\]
Splitting products of sums according as the two indices are ordered or equal gives the exact stuffle identities
\[
 V=\frac{Q^2-R}{2},                                      \tag{1}
\]
\[
 X+W=HC-R,                                                \tag{2}
\]
and, directly from \(H_1(k)^2=H_2(k)+2e_2(k)\),
\[
 A=V+2E.                                                  \tag{3}
\]

We first establish the harmonic divisibility information needed later.

For \(1\leq m\leq p-2\),
\[
 H_m=O(p).                                                \tag{4}
\]
To see this, reduce modulo \(p\). In \(\mathbb F_p\), inversion permutes the nonzero elements, so \(H_m\) has the same residue as \(\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p^\times}x^m\). If \(g\) is a generator of the cyclic group \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), this is the geometric sum
\(\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}g^{mj}\), which is zero because \(p-1\nmid m\). Thus, in particular,
\[
 Q=O(p),\qquad R=O(p).                                   \tag{5}
\]

Reflection under \(k\mapsto p-k\) supplies stronger estimates. For \(1\leq k<p\), the exact finite expansion
\[
 \frac1{p-k}=-\frac1k-\frac p{k^2}-\frac{p^2}{k^3}
              -\frac{p^3}{k^4}
              +\frac{p^4}{k^4(p-k)}                     \tag{6}
\]
follows after multiplying by \(k^4(p-k)\). Summing (6), and using that reflection permutes \(1,\ldots,p-1\), yields
\[
 2H+pQ+p^2C+p^3R=O(p^4).                                 \tag{7}
\]
Squaring the expansion through order \(p^2\) gives
\[
 \frac1{(p-k)^2}=\frac1{k^2}+\frac{2p}{k^3}
                   +\frac{3p^2}{k^4}+O(p^3).
\]
After summation,
\[
 2pC+3p^2R=O(p^3).
\]
Since \(R=O(p)\) and \(2\) is a unit, this gives
\[
 C=O(p^2).                                                \tag{8}
\]
Using (5) and (8) in (7), we obtain the refined pairing congruence
\[
 2H+pQ=O(p^4),                                           \tag{9}
\]
and consequently
\[
 H=O(p^2).                                               \tag{10}
\]

We require two further relations obtained by reflecting strictly nested double sums. The involution
\[
 (a,b)\longmapsto(p-b,p-a)

takes the region \(1\leq a<b<p\) to itself. Apply it first to
\(T=\sum_{a<b}b^{-2}a^{-1}\). Expanding the reflected summand with (6), through the required order, gives
\[
 T+U+pV+2pX=O(p^2).                                      \tag{11}
\]
For completeness, the pointwise calculation is
\[
 \frac1{(p-a)^2(p-b)}
 =-\frac1{a^2b}-p\frac1{a^2b^2}-2p\frac1{a^3b}+O(p^2);
\]
summing the three displayed terms over \(a<b\) gives respectively \(-U\), \(-pV\), and \(-2pX\).

Apply the same involution to
\(W=\sum_{a<b}b^{-3}a^{-1}\). Modulo \(p\), the reflected summand is
\[
 \frac1{(p-a)^3(p-b)}\equiv\frac1{a^3b}\pmod p,
\]
which sums to \(X\). Hence
\[
 W-X=O(p).                                                \tag{12}
\]
Equations (1), (2), (5), (8), (10), and (12) now imply
\[
 V=O(p),\qquad X=O(p),\qquad W=O(p).                     \tag{13}
\]
For example, (1) gives \(V=O(p)\); (2) gives \(X+W=O(p)\), while (12) gives \(W-X=O(p)\), and division by \(2\) is allowed.

We next derive two exact finite identities that will be truncated.

First,
\[
 H=p\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac1{k^2}
       \prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac pi\right).         \tag{14}
\]
One way to prove it is to start from the elementary alternating-binomial identity
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^j\binom n{j+1}\frac1{j+1}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac1{j+1}.                           \tag{15}
\]
Identity (15) follows by induction from Pascal's identity; equivalently, integrate
\((1-(1-x)^n)/x\) from \(0\) to \(1\). Put \(n=p\), remove the final term \(j=p-1\) from both sides, and use
\[
 \binom p{k}=\frac pk\binom{p-1}{k-1},
 \qquad
 (-1)^{k-1}\binom{p-1}{k-1}
 =\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac pi\right).
\]
This gives (14).

Second, a finite Vandermonde identity gives
\[
 p=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\prod_{i=1}^{k}
       \left(1-\frac{p^2}{i^2}\right).                  \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, the alternating convolution
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{m}(-1)^k\binom mk\binom{n+k}{k+r}
   =(-1)^m\binom n{m+r}                                  \tag{17}
\]
follows from Pascal's identity by induction on \(m\). Taking \(m=p-1,n=p,r=0\), using that \(p-1\) is even and \(\binom p{p-1}=p\), and factoring
\[
 (-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}\binom{p+k}{k}
 =\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac pi\right)
                   \left(1+\frac pi\right),
\]
yields (16).

We now truncate (14). For any finite collection \(x_i\),
\[
 \prod_i(1+cx_i)
 =1+c\sum_i x_i+c^2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j+O(c^3),              \tag{18}
\]
where here an omitted term containing \(c^r\) is \(O(p^r)\) when \(c=O(p)\). Applying (18) to (14) gives
\[
 H=pQ-p^2T+p^3E+O(p^4).                                  \tag{19}
\]

Likewise, truncate each product in (16), now with \(c=-p^2\), through its quadratic term. If
\(Q_k=H_2(k+1)\) and \(R_k=H_4(k+1)\), then
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac{p^2}{i^2}\right)
 =1-p^2Q_k+p^4\frac{Q_k^2-R_k}{2}+O(p^6).
\]
The prefix-sum interchange
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\sum_{j=1}^{k}F(j)
 =\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}(p-j)F(j)                              \tag{20}
\]
gives
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}Q_k=pQ-H,                               \tag{21}
\]
and, using
\[
 \frac{Q_k^2-R_k}{2}=\sum_{1\leq a<b\leq k}\frac1{a^2b^2},
\]
the same interchange gives
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{Q_k^2-R_k}{2}=pV-U.              \tag{22}
\]
Substitution in (16), followed by cancellation of the initial \(p\), gives
\[
 (pQ-H)-p^2(pV-U)=O(p^4).                                \tag{23}
\]
Combining (19) and (23) yields
\[
 T+U-p(E+V)=O(p^2).                                      \tag{24}
\]
Subtract (24) from (11). We obtain
\[
 p(E+2V+2X)=O(p^2).
\]
Thus \(E+2V+2X=O(p)\), and (13) finally gives the important estimate
\[
 E=O(p).                                                 \tag{25}
\]
By (3), this also gives
\[
 A=O(p).                                                 \tag{26}
\]

We now expand the two factors in \(a(p)\).

The basic binomial product formulas are
\[
 \binom{2p-1}{p-1}=\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}\left(1+\frac pi\right), \tag{27}
\]
\[
 \binom{3p}{p}=3\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}\left(1+\frac{2p}{i}\right), \tag{28}
\]
\[
 \binom{3p-1}{2p}=\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}\left(1+\frac{2p}{i}\right), \tag{29}
\]
and, for \(1\leq k<p\),
\[
 \binom{p+k-1}{k}=\frac pk
      \prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\left(1+\frac pi\right).         \tag{30}
\]
All follow immediately by writing the factorial ratios as products and extracting the indicated exceptional factor.

The elementary-symmetric expansion through fourth degree, together with (5), (8), (10), implies the useful squared-product formula
\[
 \left(\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}\left(1+\frac ci\right)\right)^2
 =1+2cH-c^2Q+O(p^5)                                     \tag{31}
\]
whenever \(c=O(p)\). Here is why no term has been hidden improperly. The elementary symmetric functions of degrees \(2,3,4\) in \(1,1/2,\ldots,1/(p-1)\) are
\[
 e_2=\frac{H^2-Q}{2},
\]
\[
 e_3=\frac{H^3-3HQ+2C}{6},
\]
\[
 e_4=\frac{H^4-6H^2Q+3Q^2+8HC-6R}{24}.
\]
From (5), (8), and (10), these are respectively \(O(p),O(p^2),O(p)\). Expanding the square of
\(1+cH+c^2e_2+c^3e_3+c^4e_4\), the displayed terms reduce to \(1+2cH-c^2Q\), while every remaining term is \(O(p^5)\). Since \(p\geq7\), the denominators \(2,6,24\) are units.

Applying (31) to (27) and (29) gives
\[
 \binom{2p-1}{p-1}^2
 =1+2pH-p^2Q+O(p^5),                                    \tag{32}
\]
\[
 \binom{3p-1}{2p}^2
 =1+4pH-4p^2Q+O(p^5).                                   \tag{33}
\]
Using the unsquared fourth-degree product expansion in (28), with the same bounds, gives
\[
 \binom{3p}{p}=3+6pH-6p^2Q+O(p^5).                      \tag{34}
\]
For example, the apparent additional quadratic contribution is \(12p^2e_2=6p^2(H^2-Q)\); its \(6p^2H^2\) part is \(O(p^6)\), leaving \(-6p^2Q\). The cubic and quartic terms are also \(O(p^5)\).

It remains to expand
\[
 S(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{2p}\binom{p+k-1}{k}^2.
\]
Split its range into the five blocks
\[
 \begin{aligned}
S(p)={}&1
 +\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\binom{p+k-1}{k}^2
 +\binom{2p-1}{p-1}^2\\
&+\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\binom{2p+j-1}{p+j}^2
 +\binom{3p-1}{2p}^2.                                   \tag{35}
 \end{aligned}
\]
(The middle singleton is originally \(k=p\), and symmetry replaces \(\binom{2p-1}{p}\) by \(\binom{2p-1}{p-1}\).)

For the second block, (30) and the quadratic product truncation give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\binom{p+k-1}{k}^2
 ={}&p^2Q+2p^3T+p^4A+2p^4E+O(p^5).                     \tag{36}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 \left(\prod_{i<k}(1+p/i)\right)^2
 =1+2pH_1(k)+p^2\bigl(H_1(k)^2+2e_2(k)\bigr)+O(p^3),
\]
and multiplying by \(p^2/k^2\) and summing gives exactly (36).

For the fourth block, factorial cancellation gives, for \(1\leq j<p\),
\[
 \binom{2p+j-1}{p+j}
 =\frac{2p}{j}
   \left(\prod_{u=1}^{j-1}\left(1+\frac{2p}{u}\right)\right)
   \left(\prod_{t=j+1}^{p-1}\left(1+\frac pt\right)\right). \tag{37}
\]
To expand its square, write
\[
 h=H_1(j),\quad q=H_2(j),\quad
 y=\sum_{t=j+1}^{p-1}\frac1t,\quad
 z=\sum_{t=j+1}^{p-1}\frac1{t^2}.
\]
The two products in (37), through degree two, multiply and square to
\[
 1+2p(2h+y)
 +p^2\left((2h+y)^2+2\left(\frac{y^2-z}{2}
       +4\frac{h^2-q}{2}+2hy\right)\right)+O(p^3).       \tag{38}
\]
Now
\[
 y=H-h- rac1j,\qquad z=Q-q- rac1{j^2}.
\]
Substituting these into (38), multiplying by \(4p^2/j^2\), and summing over \(j\), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\binom{2p+j-1}{p+j}^2
={}&4p^2Q+8p^3T\\
&+8p^3(HQ-C)\\
&+4p^4\bigl(2A-4W+3R-3V+4HT-4HC
 +(2H^2-Q)Q\bigr)+O(p^5).                              \tag{39}
 \end{aligned}
\]
This formula is just the term-by-term sum of the polynomial resulting from (38): the sums of \(j^{-2}\), \(j^{-2}h\), \(j^{-3}\), \(j^{-2}h^2\), \(j^{-3}h\), and \(j^{-2}q\) are respectively \(Q,T,C,A,W,V\).

All terms on the second and third lines of (39) are \(O(p^5)\). For the second line this follows from \(H=O(p^2)\) and \(C=O(p^2)\). In the bracket on the third line, \(A,W,R,V\) are \(O(p)\); terms containing \(H\) are even smaller; and \((2H^2-Q)Q=O(p^2)\). Therefore
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\binom{2p+j-1}{p+j}^2
 =4p^2Q+8p^3T+O(p^5).                                   \tag{40}
\]

Insert (32), (33), (36), and (40) into (35). The terms in \(p^2Q\) cancel:
\[
 p^2Q-p^2Q+4p^2Q-4p^2Q=0.
\]
The two diagonal blocks contribute \(6pH\), and the two non-diagonal blocks contribute \(10p^3T\). The remaining terms from (36) are
\(p^4A+2p^4E=O(p^5)\) by (25) and (26). Hence
\[
 S(p)=3+6pH+10p^3T+O(p^5).                              \tag{41}
\]

Set
\[
 \alpha=6pH-6p^2Q,
 \qquad
 \beta=6pH+10p^3T.
\]
Equations (34) and (41) say
\[
 \binom{3p}{p}=3+\alpha+O(p^5),
 \qquad S(p)=3+\beta+O(p^5).                            \tag{42}
\]
By (5) and (10),
\[
 \alpha=O(p^3),\qquad\beta=O(p^3).                      \tag{43}
\]
The crucial linear combination is of still higher order:
\[
 4\alpha+3\beta=O(p^5).                                 \tag{44}
\]
To prove (44), first multiply (19) by \(30p\):
\[
 30pH-30p^2Q+30p^3T-30p^4E=O(p^5).
\]
Next multiply (9) by \(6p\):
\[
 12pH+6p^2Q=O(p^5).
\]
Finally, \(30p^4E=O(p^5)\) by (25). Adding these three relations gives
\[
 42pH-24p^2Q+30p^3T=O(p^5),
\]
and the left side is exactly \(4\alpha+3\beta\).

We may now finish the main case. From (42), multiplication and taking fixed powers preserve the error \(O(p^5)\), because all displayed quantities are \(p\)-integral. Thus
\[
 a(p)=\binom{3p}{p}^4S(p)^3
      =(3+\alpha)^4(3+\beta)^3+O(p^5).
\]
Because \(\alpha,\beta=O(p^3)\), every term of total degree at least two in \(\alpha,\beta\) is \(O(p^6)\). The constant and linear terms are therefore
\[
 (3+\alpha)^4(3+\beta)^3
 =3^7+3^6(4\alpha+3\beta)+O(p^6).
\]
By (44), the second term is \(O(p^5)\). Consequently
\[
 a(p)=2187+O(p^5).
\]
Since \(a(p)-2187\) is an integer, this proves
\[
 a(p)\equiv a(1)\pmod{p^5}
\]
for every prime \(p\geq7\).

It remains only to check the primes allowed by the statement but excluded from the harmonic argument. Direct evaluation of the defining finite sums gives
\[
 a(3)=202402468703748096
     =2187+3^5\cdot832931969974263,
\]
and
\[
 a(5)=587835594121137662072707812564687
     =2187+5^5\cdot188107390118764051863266500020.
\]
Thus the required congruence also holds for \(p=3\) and \(p=5\). These are all primes at least \(3\), completing the proof.
